dives.narrative: The pair at the Michigan Avenue entrance arrived in 1894. Sculptor Edward Kemeys gave each animal a character of its own. Compare their heads, tails and front paws from the sidewalk. The lion north of the steps is on the prowl. Its southern partner stands its ground.

timeline.title: Bronze lions take their places at the entrance

dives.narrative: Kate Buckingham gave Chicago the fountain in memory of her brother Clarence. The great basin stands for Lake Michigan. Look for the groups of sculpted sea horses around it. Each marks one of the four states along the lake’s shore.

Anish Kapoor’s sculpture looks like one piece of metal. Its skin actually took 168 stainless steel plates, welded and polished until their joints disappeared. Walk toward the hollow beneath the arch and watch how the curved surface rearranges the surrounding buildings.

Frank Lloyd Wright designed this Hyde Park home for Frederick Robie. It was finished in 1910. Follow the line of a projecting roof back to the wall, then look at the bands of windows and long runs of brick below. The horizontal pattern repeats at each scale.

Look up from the river at the round towers of Marina City. Cars occupy the open lower floors. Higher up, wedge-shaped apartments meet the air at curved balconies. Architect Bertrand Goldberg gathered homes and parking around the same central cores so people could live downtown.

Look up the face of the former Sears headquarters. At its base, nine square structural tubes stand together, each 75 feet wide. They end at different heights. The steps you see in the skyline trace the building’s frame.

William Wrigley Jr. chose the north bank of the river for his chewing gum company’s headquarters. Two buildings make up the complex, both faced in white terra cotta. Look at the tower above them. Its design draws on the Giralda in Seville, Spain.

The bridge had to clear the East River while meeting low ground on either bank. That explains why the approaches reach so far into Brooklyn and Manhattan. Its stone towers carry a suspension span completed in 1883 after work began in 1869.
dives.source: New York City Department of Transportation

dives.narrative: The Empire State Building opened on May 1, 1931. A button pressed by President Herbert Hoover in Washington switched on the lights. The 102-story tower had gone up in a year and 45 days, with workers adding about four and a half stories of steel framing a week.

Workers built the statue in France and took it apart for the Atlantic crossing. It arrived in New York in 1885 and was reassembled on its pedestal for the dedication in October 1886. From the harbor, compare the figure with the pedestal beneath it. The pedestal is slightly taller.

The Declaration of Independence was approved in this room in 1776. The carved chair at its front came later. John Folwell made it for Pennsylvania’s legislative speaker in 1779, and George Washington used it while presiding over the Constitutional Convention in 1787.

This was the bell of the Pennsylvania State House. Its inscription called for liberty throughout the land. Abolitionists took up that language, and advocates for women’s voting rights and civil rights later found their own cause in the same words.

When the railroad bought the block for a terminal, the merchants wanted to stay. Their new market opened beneath the train shed in 1893. Stalls occupied the street level while refrigerated rooms below held food at different temperatures. Shoppers once heard trains move overhead.

timeline.title: The market opens below the tracks

dives.narrative: The Bureau of Prisons took over a former Army prison on the island. Its distance from shore suited officials who wanted to limit contact with the outside world. Alcatraz operated as a federal penitentiary from 1934 to 1963.

Coit Tower rose on Telegraph Hill in 1933. The next year, artists working for the federal Public Works of Art Project painted its base with scenes of California during the Depression. Look at the building from both distances. The column marks the skyline, while the murals tell stories at eye level.
dives.source: San Francisco Recreation and Park Department

dives.narrative: The fabricated steel arrived with a reddish protective primer. Seeing the towers go up, consulting architect Irving Morrow investigated how that warm color looked from the bay. His studies led to International Orange, chosen to stand out against water and sky while fitting the hills.
dives.source: Golden Gate Bridge, Highway and Transportation District

dives.narrative: Seattle created a public farmers market on Pike Place in 1907. Decades later its future was in doubt. Voters approved a historic district around the market, protecting a place where producers and shoppers could still meet in the middle of the city.

Stand where you can see the base of Rainier Tower in profile. Minoru Yamasaki’s design places 29 office floors above an eleven-story concrete pedestal. The pedestal curves inward as it descends, leaving an open space where the edges of a conventional office tower would meet the block.

Hal Griffith wanted to bring a Ferris wheel to Seattle for nearly thirty years. He eventually built one on his own pier. From the waterfront, trace the circle of 42 enclosed gondolas and look for the point where the deck beneath them gives way to Elliott Bay.

Lyman Cornelius Smith bought the lot at Second and Yesler in 1899. Plans for a modest tower grew more ambitious before construction began. When Smith Tower opened on July 4, 1914, thousands of visitors rode the elevator to an observatory on the 35th floor.

timeline.title: The observatory welcomes its first visitors

dives.narrative: The tower was conceived for Seattle’s 1962 World’s Fair. Architect John Graham Jr. developed the flying-saucer form at the top. Victor Steinbrueck drew on a sculpture of a dancer for the narrow waist of the supporting structure. Trace the two shapes separately from the ground.

From the plaza, look beyond the front row of columns to the sides of the memorial. Thirty-six columns surround the building, one for each state in the Union at Lincoln’s death. Above them, the state names appear in the frieze.

Viewed from the Mall, the Capitol’s dome seems to grow from the masonry below. Architect Thomas U. Walter designed it in cast iron. Follow its silhouette from the wide base to the statue at the top and imagine how workers assembled the many pieces over the Rotunda.

Maya Lin set the memorial’s polished black granite walls into the ground. As the path descends, the panels rise beside it. The names follow the dates of the service members’ deaths or disappearances, making the progression of the war part of the walk.

Look for the horizontal change in color on the monument’s shaft. Work stopped in 1854 when money ran out. The stone for the later part came from another quarry, and those blocks weathered differently. The pale bands on an apparently uniform obelisk mark two periods of work.

timeline.title: Construction halts for lack of funding

tours.blurb: From the river to Grant Park, see how architects and artists put a parking garage, a skyline, two lions and a lake into four very different forms.

tours.title: Millennium Moments

tour_stop.note: Start on the river side with both towers in view. Find the floor where the open spiral of parked cars changes into rings of balconies.
Before approaching the arch, pick a building in the reflected skyline. Take a few steps to one side and see whether you can keep track of it.
At the Michigan Avenue steps, compare the two lions from the sidewalk. Which one looks ready to move? Look at the forepaws before you decide.
Finish at the basin in Grant Park. Walk part of its rim to spot the separate groups of sea horses that stand for the states around Lake Michigan.

tours.blurb: Start at the Space Needle and finish at Rainier Tower. In between, descend to the market and waterfront to see what Seattle built around the edge of Elliott Bay.

tours.title: Emerald City Sampler

tour_stop.note: Begin at Seattle Center. Trace the legs as they narrow at the waist and widen again to support the saucer.
At the market, look at how the stalls meet the street. Imagine a farmer bringing produce here in 1907 to sell directly to neighbors.
Down on the waterfront, stand back far enough to see both the wheel and its pier. Look for the point on the rim that extends over the water.
Head inland for the final stop. Look up from across the street and trace the outline of the tower down to its narrow concrete base.

tours.blurb: Go east to the Capitol before crossing back toward the Lincoln Memorial. Stone, iron and polished granite tell four different stories along this long Mall walk.

tours.title: National Mall Postcards

tour_stop.note: Begin near the obelisk. Shade your eyes and scan the stone for the line where the marble changes shade.
Head east along the Mall. As the dome grows larger, look for the change from the straight lines of the building to the curves of the cast-iron dome.
Return west to the memorial. Follow the path quietly as the ground slopes down and the walls fill more of your field of view.
Finish at the Lincoln Memorial. From the plaza, pick out the rows of columns on the sides before looking back along the Mall.
